intro: Long ago, some people joined groups that kept a secret. In Greece, thousands walked to a town called Eleusis for holy rites. They promised never to tell what they saw. In the Roman world, small groups of men met in dark, cave-like rooms to honor a god named Mithras. In southern Italy, a teacher named Pythagoras led a brotherhood that loved numbers.

These groups left very little writing about their secrets. So how do we know anything about them? We look at old buildings, floors, carvings and poems. We read what visitors and enemies wrote. Then we sort what is well supported from what is only a legend.

In this unit, you will walk the Sacred Way, climb the seven steps of Mithras and try a Pythagorean number rule. By the end, you will be able to explain why people joined these groups. You will also be able to use evidence to tell a fact from a story told later.
bigQuestion: How can we learn the truth about ancient groups that worked hard to keep their secrets?

timeline.t: The Hymn to Demeter tells the story of Demeter, Persephone and the rites at Eleusis.
Pythagoras leads a brotherhood of followers at Croton, in southern Italy.
Athens is upset when young men are accused of acting out the Mysteries at parties.
A woman named Ninnion gives a painted clay tablet to the goddesses of Eleusis.
The travel writer Pausanias visits Eleusis but will not describe what is inside.
A mithraeum is built in Rome, in the place where San Clemente church stands today.
The London Mithraeum is built beside the Walbrook river.
The Felicissimus mithraeum at Ostia gets its seven-grade mosaic floor.
Emperor Theodosius makes a law against the old rites. The Mysteries soon end.
Diggers find the mithraeum deep beneath the church of San Clemente in Rome.
Archaeologists find the marble head of Mithras on the last day of a dig in London.
The rebuilt London Mithraeum opens to visitors.

the secret rites held at Eleusis, open only to people who had joined
a holy place with temples and altars, set apart from everyday life
a large group of people walking together for a special reason
a serious promise, often made in a holy way
the high priest of Eleusis; the name means one who shows the holy things
a small, cave-like room where followers of Mithras met
a rank or level in a group; members move up from one grade to the next
a picture made of many small pieces of stone or glass set close together
a close group of people who treat each other like family and share rules
a story told for a long time that cannot be proven true
facts or objects that help show what is true

test.q: Which goddess of grain was honored at Eleusis?
test.why: The Mysteries of Eleusis honored Demeter, goddess of grain, and her daughter Persephone.

test.q: What did every initiate at Eleusis promise?
test.why: Every initiate made a vow of silence about what was shown and said inside the hall.

test.q: About how long was the walk from Athens to Eleusis?
test.why: The Sacred Way from Athens to Eleusis was about 13 miles long.

test.q: In what building did the most secret rites at Eleusis take place?
test.why: The Telesterion was the huge hall at Eleusis where the secret rites happened.

test.q: Why did the Mysteries of Eleusis end in the late 300s CE?
choices: Roman laws closed the old rites and the sanctuary was wrecked
test.why: In 392 CE Emperor Theodosius passed a law against the old rites, and in 396 CE the sanctuary was wrecked.

test.q: Which is the best reason the secret of Eleusis is still unknown?
choices: The Ninnion Tablet shows it all
Pausanias told it in his book
Initiates kept their promise of silence
test.why: Initiates kept their vow, and even writers like Pausanias stopped before telling it.

test.q: What were the rooms where followers of Mithras met like?
choices: Small, dark rooms made to feel like caves
test.why: Mithraea were small, dark, cave-like rooms with benches along the sides.

test.q: Which kinds of people joined the groups of Mithras?
choices: Men such as soldiers, traders and enslaved or freed workers
test.why: Most scholars think only men joined; many were soldiers, and others were traders, officials, and enslaved or freed men.

test.q: What does the Felicissimus floor at Ostia show?
choices: The seven grades of Mithras members
A map of the Sacred Way
test.why: The mosaic floor has seven panels, one for each grade, with symbols and planets.

test.q: How are the Ninnion Tablet and the Felicissimus mosaic alike?
choices: Both show the final secret of Eleusis
Both are pictures that give clues about secret groups
test.why: The tablet gives clues about Eleusis, and the mosaic gives clues about the grades of Mithras.

test.q: What happened in London on 18 September 1954?
choices: The marble head of Mithras was found
The Ostia floor was dug up
test.why: On the last planned day of the Walbrook dig, the team found the marble head of Mithras.

test.q: What did later writers say new Pythagorean members had to do?
choices: Stay silent and listen for a long time
test.why: Later writers say new members stayed silent for a long time, some say five years, before speaking.

test.q: What does Plimpton 322 teach us about the Pythagorean theorem?
choices: The rule was known in Babylon long before Pythagoras
It was found under San Clemente
It was a secret of Eleusis
test.why: The Babylonian tablet lists number sets that fit the rule, more than a thousand years before Pythagoras.

test.q: Which of these is a legend?
choices: Hippasus was punished for sharing a math secret
The London Mithraeum was found in 1954
The Mysteries ended in the late 300s CE
test.why: The Hippasus story comes only from late writers with no earlier record, so historians call it a legend.

test.q: Why do historians read Tertullian and Clement of Alexandria with care?
choices: They opposed the religions they wrote about
test.why: Both were Christian writers who opposed these religions, so their reports may be one-sided.

write.prompt: Which group kept its secrets better: the initiates of Eleusis, the followers of Mithras, or the Pythagoreans? Make a claim. Use two or three facts or sources from this unit to support it, and explain your thinking.
tips: Start with one clear sentence that states your claim.
Name your sources, such as the Hymn to Demeter, Pausanias, the Ostia floor or Polybius.
Say what we know for sure and what is only a legend.
Use unit words like initiate, vow, mithraeum and evidence.
Be fair: say one thing the other groups did well, too.

title: Mystery Rites of the Ancient World

chapters.title: The Mysteries of Eleusis
chapters.bigQuestion: How did thousands of people keep one secret for more than a thousand years?

story.title: The Walk to Eleusis
story.kicker: A young woman from Athens joins thousands of walkers on a road that leads to a secret.
paragraphs: It is autumn in Athens, about 2,400 years ago. A young woman we will call Melissa stands in a huge crowd. Her mother stands beside her. Many people wear crowns of green leaves. Some carry long torches. Today they will walk the Sacred Way to a town called Eleusis.

The road is long, about 13 miles. The walkers sing. They call out the names of the gods. They pass farms and olive trees. Near the end, they see the blue sea. Melissa's feet hurt. But she keeps going. She has waited a long time for this day.

Night falls as the crowd reaches Eleusis. Torches light up a great stone hall. Melissa has made a promise. She will never tell what she sees inside. Thousands of people around her have made the same promise.

Later, Melissa walks home. She feels calm and full of hope. Friends ask her what happened inside the hall. She only smiles. Her secret is safe. Even today, historians do not know exactly what she saw. Melissa is a made-up person, but walks like hers really happened every year.
story.think: Why do you think Melissa kept her promise, even when her friends asked her what happened?

sections.title: A Holy Place and Its Story

lessons.title: A Holy Place Near Athens
lessons.mainIdea: Eleusis was a holy place near Athens where secret rites, called the Mysteries, were held for more than a thousand years.
reading: Eleusis is a town in Greece, about 13 miles west of the city of Athens. Long ago, Eleusis had a *sanctuary*. A sanctuary is a holy place with temples and altars. Strong walls kept it apart from the busy world outside.

Every year, people came to Eleusis for secret rites called the *Mysteries*. A rite is a set of holy actions done in a special order. Only people who had joined could see the most secret part. A person who joins through a special ceremony is called an *initiate*.

The Mysteries lasted more than a thousand years. Historians have strong evidence for them from the 500s BCE to the late 300s CE. Some think they began even earlier. Very few traditions in history have lasted that long.

words.d: a holy place with temples and altars, set apart from everyday life
the secret rites held at Eleusis, open only to people who had joined
a person who has joined a group through a special ceremony

look.title: A Map in Words
look.text: Picture a map of Greece. Find the big city of Athens near the sea. Now move your finger west, along the coast, about 13 miles. Stop at a small town beside a bay. That is Eleusis. A road runs between the two places. People called it the Sacred Way.
look.prompt: About how far was Eleusis from Athens? Name a place about that far from your school.

check.q: What is a sanctuary?
choices: A holy place with temples and altars
A long road between two towns
A secret word used by initiates
A crown made of green leaves
check.why: The reading says a sanctuary is a holy place with temples and altars.

check.q: About how long did the Mysteries of Eleusis last?
check.why: The reading says the Mysteries lasted more than a thousand years, from at least the 500s BCE to the late 300s CE.

check.q: What do we call a person who joins a group through a special ceremony?
check.why: An initiate is a person who has joined through a special ceremony.

lessons.title: Demeter Looks for Her Daughter
lessons.mainIdea: The Mysteries honored Demeter, goddess of grain, and her daughter Persephone, who was taken to the land of the dead.
reading: The Greeks told a *myth* about two goddesses. A myth is an old story about gods or heroes. Demeter was the goddess of grain, the plants that give us bread. Her daughter was named Persephone. One day, Hades, king of the land of the dead, carried Persephone away.

Demeter searched everywhere for her daughter. She was so sad that she stopped helping plants grow. Fields turned brown. People had no grain to eat. At last, Zeus, the king of the gods, sent a messenger to bring Persephone back.

But Persephone had eaten a few pomegranate seeds in the land of the dead. So she had to go back for part of every year. When she returned to her mother, Demeter was happy and the fields grew green. Many people later read this as a story about the seasons.

words.d: an old story about gods or heroes that people told to explain the world
the Greek goddess of grain and harvest, honored at Eleusis
Demeter's daughter, who spent part of each year in the land of the dead

look.title: Fields in Two Seasons
look.text: Picture a field in two seasons. In one picture, the wheat is tall and gold. A woman carries a basket full of grain. In the other picture, the ground is brown and bare. Nothing grows. A cold wind blows over the empty field.
look.prompt: Which picture matches the time Persephone is with her mother? Explain how the myth fits the seasons.

check.q: What was Demeter the goddess of?
check.why: Demeter was the goddess of grain, the plants that give us bread.

check.q: What happened when Demeter was sad?
choices: Plants stopped growing and fields turned brown
check.why: In the myth, Demeter stopped helping plants grow, and the fields turned brown.

check.q: Why did Persephone have to go back to the land of the dead each year?
choices: She had eaten a few pomegranate seeds there
She wanted to rule the gods
She got lost on the Sacred Way
check.why: The myth says she ate pomegranate seeds in the land of the dead, so she had to return for part of every year.

lessons.title: The Hymn That Tells the Story
lessons.mainIdea: An old Greek poem, the Hymn to Demeter, tells the myth and says the goddess herself gave the rites to Eleusis.
reading: We know the myth from an old poem called the *Hymn to Demeter*. A *hymn* is a song or poem that praises a god. Nobody knows who wrote this one. Scholars think it was made about 2,600 years ago, around 600 BCE.

In the poem, sad Demeter wanders to Eleusis. She is dressed as an old woman, so no one knows her. The people of Eleusis are kind to her. Later, she tells them to build her a temple. There she teaches the leaders of the town her holy rites.

The hymn says the rites must not be told to others. It also says the people who have seen them are happy, or blessed. So the poem gives two big ideas at once: keep the secret, and the secret brings hope.

words.d: a song or poem that praises a god
an old Greek poem, from about 600 BCE, that tells the story of Demeter and Eleusis

look.title: What the Hymn Promises
look.text: Happy is the person on earth who has seen these rites. But the person who has not taken part will not have the same good share after death, down in the dark.
look.cite: Homeric Hymn to Demeter, about 600 BCE, near the end of the poem; retold from the translation by Hugh G. Evelyn-White, 1914
look.prompt: What does the hymn promise to people who have seen the rites? Why might that make someone want to join?

check.q: What is a hymn?
choices: A map of a holy place
A song or poem that praises a god
check.why: The reading explains that a hymn is a song or poem that praises a god.

check.q: How was Demeter dressed when she came to Eleusis in the poem?
check.why: In the Hymn to Demeter, she is dressed as an old woman, so no one knows her.

check.q: What two big ideas does the hymn give about the rites?
choices: Share them widely, and they bring money
Keep them secret, and they bring hope
Change them often, and they bring rain
Write them down, and they bring fame
check.why: The hymn says the rites must not be told, and it calls the people who saw them happy or blessed.

lessons.title: Who Could Join
lessons.mainIdea: The Mysteries were open to many kinds of people: men and women, rich and poor, free and enslaved, if they spoke Greek.
reading: Many Greek holy events were only for citizens of one city. Eleusis was different. Men and women could join. Rich and poor people could join. Even enslaved people could join. This made the Mysteries very unusual.
There were a few rules. A person had to understand Greek, so they could follow the words of the rites. A person who had killed someone could not join. Everyone else was welcome to begin.

Joining took steps. First, a person took part in smaller rites in the spring. Then, months later, they could come to the great rites in the autumn. Each new initiate had a guide who had already been through it. This guide was called a *mystagogue*.

words.d: a guide who had already joined and helped a new person through the Mysteries
forced to work for others without freedom or pay

look.title: Three People at the Gate
look.text: Three people stand at the gate. The first is a rich man from Athens. The second is a woman who sells bread in the market. The third is an enslaved worker from a farm. All three speak Greek. None of them has ever hurt anyone.
look.prompt: Using the rules in the reading, which of these three people could begin the Mysteries? Explain your answer.

check.q: What made the Mysteries of Eleusis unusual?
choices: Many kinds of people could join, even enslaved people
check.why: The reading says men, women, rich, poor and even enslaved people could join, which was unusual.

check.q: What did a person need to understand to join?
check.why: A person had to understand Greek to follow the words of the rites.

check.q: What was a mystagogue?
choices: A guide who helped a new initiate
check.why: A mystagogue was a guide who had already joined and helped a new person.

lessons.title: Walking the Sacred Way
lessons.mainIdea: In autumn, thousands of people walked about 13 miles from Athens to Eleusis in a great procession.
reading: The great rites came each autumn and lasted several days. First, the people gathered in Athens. They washed in the sea to make themselves clean for the goddess. Then came the most famous day: the long walk.

A *procession* is a large group walking together for a special reason. Thousands of people walked the road from Athens to Eleusis. This road was called the *Sacred Way*. It was about 13 miles long. Walkers carried torches, sang songs and called out to the gods.

The walk took most of the day. The crowd reached Eleusis as darkness fell. Walking together made strangers feel like one big group. Tired feet, shared songs and bright torches all became part of the memory.

words.d: a large group of people walking together for a special reason
the road, about 13 miles long, from Athens to Eleusis

look.title: The Road at Sunset
look.text: Picture the road at sunset. The sky is orange. Thousands of people fill the road. Some are old. Some are young. Torches glow in their hands. You can hear singing ahead and behind. Dust rises from the dry ground. Up ahead, walls and a great roof appear.
look.prompt: What would you hear, see and feel on this walk? How might walking together change how people felt about each other?

check.q: What is a procession?
choices: A large group walking together for a special reason
check.why: The reading defines a procession as a large group walking together for a special reason.

check.q: About how long was the Sacred Way?
check.why: The Sacred Way from Athens to Eleusis was about 13 miles long.

check.q: When did the walkers reach Eleusis?
check.why: The reading says the crowd reached Eleusis as darkness fell.

lessons.title: Inside the Great Hall
lessons.mainIdea: The most secret part happened in a huge hall called the Telesterion, led by a high priest called the hierophant.
reading: At Eleusis stood a huge hall called the *Telesterion*. It was built so thousands of people could be inside at once. Rows of stone steps ran along the walls. In the middle was a small, special room.

The high priest was called the *hierophant*. The word means one who shows the holy things. On the most secret night, he showed the initiates something. People said there was bright light after darkness. But nobody wrote down exactly what was shown.

Initiates also drank a special drink made of barley and mint, called the kykeon. In the myth, Demeter drank it at Eleusis. Some modern writers have guessed that a mold from grain was in the drink and changed how people felt. Many historians doubt this, and no proof has been found.

words.d: the huge hall at Eleusis where the most secret rites took place
the high priest of Eleusis; the name means one who shows the holy things

look.title: What We Know and What We Do Not
look.text: What we know: the hall was huge. Thousands of people fit inside. A high priest showed holy things. Initiates drank a barley drink. What we do not know: exactly what was shown, what words were spoken, and what people saw in the light.
look.prompt: Why do you think the list of things we do not know is about the most secret part of the night?

check.q: What was the Telesterion?
choices: The huge hall where the secret rites took place
check.why: The Telesterion was the huge hall at Eleusis where the most secret rites happened.

check.q: What does the word hierophant mean?
choices: One who shows the holy things
check.why: The reading says hierophant means one who shows the holy things.

check.q: What do historians say about the idea that the kykeon had something in it that changed how people felt?
choices: Many doubt it, and no proof has been found
It was proved by a museum
check.why: The reading says many historians doubt this idea, and no proof has been found.

lessons.title: A Promise of Silence
lessons.mainIdea: Initiates promised to keep the rites secret, and in Athens telling or mocking them was a serious crime.
reading: Every initiate made a *vow* of silence. A vow is a serious promise. They could say that they had joined. They could say that it made them happy. But they could not tell what was shown or said inside the hall.

The city of Athens made this a law. Telling the secret, or making fun of the rites, was a serious crime. In 415 BCE, some rich young men were accused of acting out the Mysteries at private parties. The whole city was upset.

One man accused was Alcibiades, a famous general. He was away at war when Athens called him home for trial. He ran away to an enemy city instead. The story shows how much the people of Athens cared about the secret.

words.d: a serious promise, often made in a holy way
said to have done something wrong, before it is proven

look.title: What May I Say?
look.text: An initiate named Nikias comes home. His neighbor asks three questions. First: Did you go to Eleusis? Second: Did it make you feel good? Third: What did the priest show you in the hall?
look.prompt: Which questions could Nikias answer, and which one must he keep secret? Use the reading to explain.

check.q: What is a vow?
check.why: The reading says a vow is a serious promise.

check.q: What were some young men in Athens accused of in 415 BCE?
choices: Acting out the Mysteries at private parties
Walking the Sacred Way at night
check.why: In 415 BCE, some rich young men were accused of acting out the Mysteries at parties.

check.q: What did Alcibiades do when Athens called him home for trial?
choices: He ran away to an enemy city
check.why: The reading says Alcibiades ran away to an enemy city instead of facing trial.

lessons.title: What Old Writers Said
lessons.mainIdea: Ancient writers often mentioned the Mysteries but stopped before telling the secret; later enemies claimed to tell parts of it.
reading: Many writers in ancient times were initiates. They wrote that the Mysteries were beautiful and gave people hope. But when they came to the secret part, they stopped. Their silence is a kind of *evidence*, too. It shows how strong the promise was.

A travel writer named Pausanias visited Greece around 160 CE. He described many temples in detail. At Eleusis, he wrote that a dream warned him not to describe what was inside the walls. So he did not.

Around 200 CE, a Christian teacher named Clement of Alexandria wrote against the old religions. He claimed to tell some secret words of the rites. Historians use his words with care. He was an enemy of the rites, and enemies do not always report fairly.

words.d: facts or objects that help show what is true
a feeling for or against something that can change how a person tells about it

look.title: A Travel Writer Stops
look.text: My dream told me not to write about the things inside the wall of the sanctuary. And it is clear that people who have not joined may not learn about what they are not allowed to see.
look.cite: Pausanias, Description of Greece, Book 1, about 160 CE; retold from the translation by W. H. S. Jones, 1918
look.prompt: Pausanias describes many temples in detail. Why does he stop here? What does that tell you about the secret?

check.q: Why did Pausanias not describe what was inside the walls at Eleusis?
choices: He wrote that a dream warned him not to
He was not able to write
check.why: Pausanias wrote that a dream warned him not to describe what was inside the walls.

check.q: Why do historians use Clement of Alexandria's words with care?
choices: He was an enemy of the rites and may not report fairly
He lived in Eleusis all his life
He wrote in a secret code
check.why: Clement wrote against the old religions, and the reading says enemies do not always report fairly. That is bias.

check.q: How can a writer's silence be evidence?
choices: It proves the rites never happened
It shows how strong the promise of secrecy was
It shows the writer was an enemy
check.why: The reading says the writers' silence shows how strong the promise was.

lessons.title: A Picture From Ninnion
lessons.mainIdea: Objects like the Ninnion Tablet give us clues about the Mysteries, but even they do not show the final secret.
reading: Around 370 BCE, a woman named Ninnion gave a gift to the goddesses of Eleusis. It was a painted clay *tablet*, a flat board with a picture on it. People gave gifts like this to say thank you to the gods.

The tablet was buried for a very long time. Archaeologists found it at Eleusis in 1895. An *archaeologist* is a person who studies the past by digging up and looking at old things. Today the tablet is in the National Archaeological Museum in Athens.

The picture shows people walking with torches toward the goddesses. It is one of the rare pictures of the Mysteries that survive. It shows the way in. But it does not show the final secret. The picture keeps the secret, too.

words.d: a flat piece of clay, stone or wood with a picture or writing on it
a person who studies the past by digging up and looking at old things

look.title: Reading the Tablet
look.text: Picture a flat clay tablet, painted red and black. People walk in a line. Some hold torches. At one side, a goddess sits. The people are walking toward her. There are no words that tell what happens next.
look.prompt: What can you learn from this picture? What is still hidden?

check.q: Who gave the painted tablet to the goddesses?
check.why: The reading says a woman named Ninnion gave the tablet around 370 BCE.

check.q: What does an archaeologist do?
choices: Studies the past by digging up old things
check.why: An archaeologist studies the past by digging up and looking at old things.

check.q: What does the Ninnion Tablet NOT show?
choices: The final secret of the rites
check.why: The tablet shows the way in, but not the final secret.

sections.title: Why People Came, and the End

lessons.title: Hope and Belonging
lessons.mainIdea: People joined the Mysteries for hope about life after death and for the feeling of belonging to something great.
reading: Why would thousands of people walk 13 miles each year? One big reason was hope. The Greeks worried about what happens after death. The Hymn to Demeter said initiates would have a better share. Many people believed it.

Another reason was *belonging*. That is the feeling of being part of a group. At Eleusis, a farmer and a rich lord walked the same road. They kept the same secret. For a few days, they were all initiates together.
Later, even famous Romans came to join. The Roman speaker Cicero was an initiate. He wrote that the Mysteries helped people live well and face death with more hope. Some Roman emperors joined, too.

words.d: the feeling of being part of a group that accepts you
a life that some people believe comes after death

look.title: Two Reasons to Go
look.text: Two friends talk about going to Eleusis. Thea says, "I want to feel less afraid of what comes after this life." Dion says, "I want to walk with everyone, from farmers to lords, and be part of something big."
look.prompt: Which friend is talking about hope for the afterlife? Which one is talking about belonging? Which reason matters more to you?

check.q: What is belonging?
choices: The feeling of being part of a group
A promise to keep a secret
A long road to a temple
check.why: The reading defines belonging as the feeling of being part of a group.

check.q: What hope did the Hymn to Demeter give initiates?
choices: That they would never get sick
That they would win every war
That they would have a better share after death
check.why: The reading says the hymn promised initiates a better share after death.

check.q: Which famous Roman was an initiate at Eleusis?
check.why: The reading says the Roman speaker Cicero was an initiate.

lessons.title: The End of the Mysteries
lessons.mainIdea: The Mysteries ended in the late 300s CE, when Roman laws closed the old religions and the sanctuary was wrecked.
reading: By the 300s CE, Greece was part of the Roman Empire. Many people in the empire had become Christians. The emperors were Christian, too. They began to make laws against the old religions.

In 392 CE, Emperor Theodosius passed a law against the old rites. A few years later, in 396 CE, an army led by a man named Alaric wrecked the sanctuary at Eleusis. After more than a thousand years, the Mysteries came to an end. We call this kind of change a *decline*.

Today you can visit Eleusis. You can walk among the broken stones of the great hall. There is a small museum. But the secret went away with the last initiates. It is one of the best-kept secrets in history.

words.d: many lands and peoples ruled by one government or ruler
a slow change in which something gets weaker or smaller

look.title: How Long Ago?
look.cite: Dates from Helene P. Foley, The Homeric Hymn to Demeter, Princeton University Press, 1994, and the National Archaeological Museum, Athens
look.prompt: Which event happened longest ago? About how many years passed between the tablet being given and being found?

check.q: In what year did Emperor Theodosius pass a law against the old rites?
check.why: The reading says Theodosius passed the law in 392 CE.

check.q: What is an empire?
choices: A small town by the sea
Many lands and peoples ruled by one ruler
A song that praises a god
check.why: An empire is many lands and peoples ruled by one government or ruler, like the Roman Empire.

check.q: What happened to the secret of Eleusis when the rites ended?
choices: It went away with the last initiates
It was carved on the walls
It was printed in a book
It was painted on the Ninnion Tablet
check.why: The reading says the secret went away with the last initiates.

review.q: Which two goddesses were honored in the Mysteries of Eleusis?
review.why: The Mysteries honored Demeter, goddess of grain, and her daughter Persephone.

choices: The road from Athens to Eleusis
review.why: The Sacred Way was the road, about 13 miles long, that ran from Athens to Eleusis.

review.q: Who led the most secret part of the rites?
review.why: The hierophant, the high priest, showed the holy things in the Telesterion.

review.q: Which old poem tells the story of Demeter coming to Eleusis?
review.why: The Hymn to Demeter, from about 600 BCE, tells the myth and the start of the rites.

review.q: Which source is a painted clay picture found at Eleusis in 1895?
review.why: The Ninnion Tablet, given around 370 BCE, was found at Eleusis in 1895.

review.q: How are Pausanias and Clement of Alexandria different?
choices: Pausanias kept the secret; Clement, an enemy of the rites, claimed to tell parts of it
Pausanias was a priest; Clement was a king
Both told the whole secret clearly
Both were high priests at Eleusis
review.why: Pausanias stopped because of a dream; Clement wrote against the rites and claimed to reveal some words.

review.q: Which was NOT a rule for joining the Mysteries?
choices: You could not have killed someone
You had to be a rich man from Athens
You went through smaller rites first
review.why: Men and women, rich and poor, free and enslaved could join. Being rich was not a rule.

review.q: Why do historians still not know exactly what happened in the great hall?
choices: Initiates kept their vow of silence
review.why: Initiates promised silence, and the secret mostly held for more than a thousand years.

chapters.title: Mithras and Pythagoras
chapters.bigQuestion: How can we learn about a secret group that left almost no writing of its own?

story.title: The Last Day of the Dig
story.kicker: On the final day of a dig in London, a face from the Roman world comes up out of the mud.
paragraphs: It is September 1954 in London. The city is still rebuilding after World War II. On a street called Walbrook, builders plan a big new office building. Before they pour concrete, a team of archaeologists gets a short time to dig.

The team is led by W. F. Grimes and Audrey Williams. Deep in the ground, they have found the walls of a small Roman building. It is long and narrow, with a rounded end. Saturday, 18 September, is supposed to be the last day of the dig.

Then someone on the team sees something pale in the dark, wet mud. They lift it out with care. It is a marble head of a young man. He wears a soft cap that folds forward at the top. His face looks calm. He has been buried for about 1,700 years.

The news spreads fast. Long lines of Londoners come to see the old building. The head belongs to Mithras, a god that some Romans worshipped in secret. People start to ask: who met in this small, dark room? And what did they do there?
story.think: The team almost missed the head because it was the last day. What does this story tell you about how archaeology works?

lessons.title: Who Was Mithras?
lessons.mainIdea: Mithras was a god worshipped in secret by small groups of men across the Roman Empire, and his main picture shows him holding down a bull.
reading: About 1,900 years ago, some men in Roman towns met in secret to worship a god called *Mithras*. In pictures, Mithras is a young man. He wears a soft, pointed cap and a cape that flies out behind him. The most famous scene shows him holding down a bull.

This bull scene was in almost every meeting place. Two helpers with torches stand beside Mithras. One holds his torch up. The other holds his torch down. The Sun and the Moon often watch from above. Members knew what the scene meant. They did not write it down for us.

The name Mithra came from Persia, a land far to the east. But scholars disagree about how much of this religion came from Persia. Many now think it was mostly made in the Roman world, using a Persian name. This is a *debate*, and it is not settled.

words.d: a god worshipped in secret by small groups of men in the Roman Empire
a discussion where people who study a question give different answers and reasons

look.title: Reading a Carved Scene
look.text: Picture a stone carving. In the middle, a young man in a pointed cap kneels on a bull. His cape blows out behind him. On the left, a helper holds a torch up high. On the right, another helper holds a torch pointing down. In the top corners are a sun and a moon.
look.prompt: The two torches point in opposite directions. What might up and down stand for? Remember that nobody knows for sure.

check.q: What does the most famous picture of Mithras show?
check.why: The reading says the most famous scene shows Mithras holding down a bull.

check.q: How do the two helpers in the bull scene hold their torches?
choices: One holds a torch up and one holds a torch down
check.why: In the scene, one helper holds his torch up and the other holds it down.

check.q: What is the debate about Mithras?
choices: How much of the religion came from Persia
check.why: Scholars disagree about how much came from Persia; many think it was mostly made in the Roman world.

lessons.title: A Room Like a Cave
lessons.mainIdea: Followers of Mithras met in small, dark, cave-like rooms called mithraea, where they shared a meal together.
reading: A meeting place for Mithras is called a *mithraeum*. More than one are called mithraea. Many were built underground or in dark rooms with no windows. Members wanted the room to feel like a cave. In their story, Mithras killed the bull in a cave.

Most mithraea were long and narrow. A raised bench ran down each side. Members lay or sat on the benches to share a *ritual meal*, a meal eaten as part of worship. At the far end was the bull scene, often lit by lamps. Most rooms held only a few dozen people.

The members left no holy book behind. So how do we know all this? We learn from the rooms, the carvings and paintings, and words carved on altars. We also learn from writers who did not like the religion. Each kind of clue tells part of the story.

words.d: a small, cave-like room where followers of Mithras met; more than one are called mithraea
a meal eaten together as part of worship

look.title: Step Inside
look.text: Picture going down a few stone steps. The air is cool. The room has no windows. Along both long walls are raised benches, like wide stone beds. Oil lamps flicker. At the far end, lamplight shines on a carving of Mithras and the bull.
look.prompt: How is this room different from a big temple with columns in the sunlight? Why might a small group want a room like this?

check.q: What is a mithraeum?
choices: A small, cave-like room where followers of Mithras met
check.why: A mithraeum is a small, cave-like meeting room for followers of Mithras.

check.q: What were the benches along the walls used for?
check.why: Members lay or sat on the benches to share a ritual meal.

check.q: Since there is no holy book, how do we learn about Mithras?
choices: From the rooms, carvings, altar words and outside writers
From a book written by Mithras
check.why: The reading lists the rooms, carvings, paintings, altar words and writers who did not like the religion.

lessons.title: Soldiers, Traders and Workers
lessons.mainIdea: Only men joined Mithras groups, and they included soldiers, traders, officials and even enslaved men, from Britain to Syria.
reading: Most scholars agree that only men joined the groups of Mithras. Many were Roman soldiers. Others were traders, government workers and enslaved or freed men. Inside the mithraeum, rich and poor members ate together at the same benches.

Mithraea have been found across the Roman Empire. They stretch from Britain in the west to Syria in the east. Soldiers moved from place to place. So did each *merchant*, a person who buys and sells goods. They seem to have carried the religion with them.

One mithraeum in Syria has a carved date. Archers from the Roman army set it up around 168 CE. This kind of carved writing is called an *inscription*. Inscriptions help us know who the members were and when they met.

words.d: a person who buys and sells goods, often traveling to do it
words carved or written on stone, metal or another hard surface

look.title: A Soldier Pushes Away a Crown
look.text: In a cave, a new soldier of Mithras is offered a crown on the tip of a sword. He is taught to push it off his head and say that Mithras is his only crown. After that, he never wears a crown again.
look.cite: Tertullian, The Chaplet (De Corona), chapter 15, about 200 CE; retold from the Ante-Nicene Fathers translation
look.prompt: Tertullian was a Christian writer who did not like this religion. What does his story tell us? Why should we read it with care?

check.q: Who could join the groups of Mithras?
check.why: Most scholars agree that only men joined the groups of Mithras.

check.q: What is an inscription?
choices: A painting on a cave wall
A song sung at a meal
Words carved on a hard surface
check.why: An inscription is words carved or written on stone, metal or another hard surface.

check.q: How did the religion of Mithras likely spread so far?
choices: Soldiers and merchants carried it as they moved
A king ordered everyone to join
check.why: The reading says soldiers and merchants moved from place to place and seem to have carried the religion.

lessons.title: Under a Church in Rome
lessons.mainIdea: Beneath the church of San Clemente in Rome, digging revealed layers of history, with a mithraeum near the bottom.
reading: San Clemente is a church in Rome. The church you walk into today was built in the 1100s. In 1857, an Irish priest named Joseph Mullooly began to dig beneath it. He found an older church underneath, from the 300s.

Below that church were even older Roman buildings. In 1867, the diggers found a mithraeum down there. It had been built in the early 200s. But water kept flooding the lowest *layer*. A tunnel to drain the water was finished in 1914. Only then could the mithraeum be fully dug out.

Today, visitors walk down stairs through three layers of time. At the bottom, they can see the benches and the altar of Mithras. They can still hear water running nearby. Digging carefully to study the past like this is called an *excavation*.

words.d: one level of something that lies on top of or under another level
careful digging to find and study things from the past

look.title: Layers Under San Clemente
look.cite: Mithraeum of San Clemente, Mithraeum.eu database; Basilica of San Clemente, Rome
look.prompt: Which layer is the oldest? Why does the oldest layer end up at the bottom?

check.q: Who began digging under San Clemente in 1857?
check.why: The Irish priest Joseph Mullooly began to dig beneath the church in 1857.

check.q: Why could the mithraeum not be fully dug out until 1914?
choices: The church would not allow it
Water kept flooding the lowest layer
check.why: Water flooded the lowest layer until a drainage tunnel was finished in 1914.

check.q: What is an excavation?
choices: Careful digging to study the past
check.why: The reading says digging carefully to study the past is called an excavation.

lessons.title: The Floor at Ostia
lessons.mainIdea: A mosaic floor in a mithraeum at Ostia shows the seven grades, or ranks, of the members of Mithras.
reading: Ostia was the port city of ancient Rome, near the mouth of the river Tiber. Ships brought grain and goods there. Many mithraea have been found in Ostia. One of them is named for a man called Felicissimus.

In 1940, archaeologists Guido and Raissa Calza dug up this mithraeum. It was built in the second half of the 200s CE. Its floor is a *mosaic*, a picture made of many tiny pieces of stone set close together.

The mosaic is divided into seven panels, one after another. Each panel stands for one *grade*, or rank, of members. Each has its own symbols and its own planet. An eighth panel names Felicissimus. It is like a ladder that members climbed, step by step.

words.d: a picture made of many small pieces of stone or glass set close together
a rank or level in a group; members move up from one grade to the next

look.title: A Ladder on the Floor
look.text: Picture a long, narrow floor made of tiny black and white stones. It is divided into boxes, one after another, like the rungs of a ladder. Each box holds small pictures, such as a cup, a torch or a moon. As you walk toward the far end of the room, you walk up the ladder.
look.prompt: Why might a group put its ranks on the floor, where members walk over them? What would that feel like?

check.q: What was Ostia?
choices: The port city of ancient Rome
check.why: Ostia was the port city of ancient Rome, near the mouth of the river Tiber.

check.q: What is a mosaic?
choices: A picture made of many tiny pieces of stone
check.why: A mosaic is a picture made of many small pieces of stone or glass set close together.

check.q: How many grades are shown on the Felicissimus floor?
check.why: The mosaic has seven panels, one for each grade, plus an eighth that names Felicissimus.

lessons.title: Seven Steps Up
lessons.mainIdea: Members of Mithras climbed seven grades, from Raven to Father, and each grade was linked to a planet.
reading: Other evidence agrees with the floor at Ostia. There were seven grades. In order, they were Raven, Bridegroom, Soldier, Lion, Persian, Runner of the Sun, and Father. The Father was the highest grade. He led the group.

Each grade had a *planet*. Romans counted seven moving lights in the sky as planets, including the Sun and the Moon. The Raven went with Mercury. The Soldier went with Mars. The Persian went with the Moon. The Runner of the Sun went with the Sun. The Father went with Saturn.

What did members do to move up a grade? We do not know for sure. The members kept that secret, and few clues survive. The grades show one clear idea, though. Belonging to the group meant growing, one step at a time.

words.d: to the Romans, one of seven moving lights in the sky, including the Sun and the Moon
a person's level or position in a group

look.title: Design Your Own Ladder
look.text: The Mithras groups named their seven steps after animals and people: Raven, Bridegroom, Soldier, Lion, Persian, Runner of the Sun and Father. Imagine a club that helps people learn to be kind. It has seven steps. Each step needs a name and a small picture.
look.prompt: Name your seven steps and draw a symbol for each. What would someone learn at each step?

check.q: What was the highest grade in the groups of Mithras?
check.why: The Father was the highest grade and led the group.

check.q: Which grade went with the planet Mars?
check.why: The reading says the Soldier went with Mars.

check.q: What do we know about how members moved up a grade?
choices: We do not know for sure
check.why: The members kept it secret, and few clues survive, so we do not know for sure.

lessons.title: The Head in the Mud
lessons.mainIdea: The London Mithraeum, found in 1954, drew huge crowds and was later rebuilt so people can visit it today.
reading: The London Mithraeum was built around the middle of the 200s CE. It stood near a small river called the Walbrook. Over hundreds of years, it was buried under mud and newer buildings. People forgot it was there.

In 1954, archaeologists W. F. Grimes and Audrey Williams dug at the site. On 18 September, the last planned day of the dig, they found the marble head of Mithras. Long lines of people came to see the temple. Many people argued that it should be saved.

The stones were moved and put back together nearby. Later, the temple was rebuilt again, on the spot where it was first found. It opened to visitors in 2017. When people build something again from its old parts, we say they *reconstruct* it.

words.d: to build something again, often from its old parts
a hard, smooth stone often used for statues

look.title: The London Mithraeum Over Time
look.cite: John D. Shepherd, The Temple of Mithras, London: Excavations by W. F. Grimes and A. Williams at the Walbrook, English Heritage, 1998; London Mithraeum Bloomberg SPACE, 2017
look.prompt: About how many years passed between when the temple was built and when the head was found?

check.q: What was found on 18 September 1954?
check.why: On the last planned day of the dig, the team found the marble head of Mithras.

check.q: What does reconstruct mean?
choices: To build something again from its old parts
check.why: To reconstruct is to build something again, often from its old parts, as London did with the temple.

check.q: When did the rebuilt London Mithraeum open to visitors?
check.why: The reading says it opened to visitors in 2017.

lessons.title: A Teacher Comes to Croton
lessons.mainIdea: Pythagoras, a Greek thinker from Samos, led a brotherhood of followers in southern Italy about 2,500 years ago.
reading: *Pythagoras* was born on Samos, a Greek island, more than 2,500 years ago. As a grown man, he moved west to a Greek city called Croton. Croton is in southern Italy. Many Greeks lived in cities there.

In Croton, Pythagoras became a teacher. People came to learn from him and to live by his rules. His followers formed a *brotherhood*, a close group who treat each other like family. Later writers say some women were followers, too. Many shared their meals and their way of life.
Pythagoras wrote no books that survive. His followers were called Pythagoreans. They studied numbers, music and how to live a good life. They kept some of their teachings inside the group.

words.d: a Greek thinker from Samos who led a brotherhood in southern Italy about 2,500 years ago
a close group of people who treat each other like family and share rules
a person who learns from a leader and lives by that leader's ideas

look.title: From an Island to Italy
look.text: Picture a map. In the east, near the coast of what is now Turkey, is a small Greek island called Samos. Far to the west, across the sea, is the toe of Italy's boot. On the sole of that boot is the city of Croton. Pythagoras made that long trip.
look.prompt: Trace the trip with your finger. Why might a teacher move to a new city to start a group?

check.q: Where was Pythagoras born?
check.why: The reading says Pythagoras was born on Samos, a Greek island.

check.q: What is a brotherhood?
choices: A close group who treat each other like family
check.why: A brotherhood is a close group of people who treat each other like family.

check.q: What did the Pythagoreans study?
choices: Numbers, music and how to live a good life
check.why: The reading says they studied numbers, music and how to live a good life.

lessons.title: Rules and Silence
lessons.mainIdea: Later writers say the Pythagoreans lived by short rules and that new members first had to listen in silence.
reading: Later writers describe strict rules for the brotherhood. They say new members had to stay silent for a long time, some say five years. They listened and learned before they could speak in the group. This kind of silence is a way to show *discipline*, or self-control.

The group also had short sayings to live by. People called them things heard, because members learned them by listening. One famous rule was: do not eat beans. Even in ancient times, people argued about why. Nobody is sure today.

A Roman writer, Cicero, said Pythagoreans ended arguments with a short phrase: He himself said it. That meant Pythagoras had said so, so the matter was closed. Some people admired this *loyalty*. Others thought people should give reasons, not just names.

words.d: self-control; following rules even when it is hard
staying true and faithful to a person or group

look.title: Short Rules to Live By
look.text: Among the rules of Pythagoras: do not stir a fire with a knife. Do not step over a scale for weighing. Stay away from beans.
look.cite: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, Book 8, about 230 CE; retold from the translation by R. D. Hicks, 1925
look.prompt: These rules sound strange. Many people think some were meant as picture-sayings with hidden meanings. What might do not stir a fire with a knife mean?

check.q: According to later writers, what did new members do at first?
check.why: Later writers say new members stayed silent for a long time and listened before they spoke.

check.q: What is discipline?
choices: Self-control, following rules even when it is hard
check.why: The reading says discipline is self-control.

check.q: What did the phrase He himself said it mean to Pythagoreans?
choices: Pythagoras had said so, so the matter was closed
check.why: Cicero said Pythagoreans used the phrase to show that Pythagoras had said so, closing the argument.

lessons.title: Numbers Everywhere
lessons.mainIdea: Pythagoreans believed numbers could explain the world, from music to shapes, though some ideas named for Pythagoras are older than him.
reading: The Pythagoreans believed numbers were the key to the whole world. They studied music this way. A shorter string plays a higher note. A string half as long plays a note that sounds the same, only higher. We call that an octave. The two lengths make a *ratio* of 2 to 1.

You may meet the Pythagorean theorem in math class. It is about a *right triangle*, a triangle with one square corner. Square the two short sides and add them. You get the square of the long side. For sides 3 and 4, that is 9 plus 16, which makes 25, or 5 times 5.

But the theorem is older than Pythagoras. A clay tablet from ancient Babylon, called Plimpton 322, lists number sets that fit this rule. It was made more than a thousand years before him. Nobody knows if Pythagoras himself proved the rule.

words.d: a way to compare two numbers, such as 2 to 1
a triangle with one square corner, like the corner of a book

look.title: The 3-4-5 Triangle
look.cite: Euclid, Elements, Book 1, Proposition 47, about 300 BCE
look.prompt: Add the first two numbers. What do you get? Try it with sides 6, 8 and 10.

check.q: What is a right triangle?
choices: A triangle with three equal sides
A triangle with one square corner
A triangle drawn on a floor
check.why: The reading says a right triangle has one square corner.

check.q: In a 3-4-5 triangle, what is 9 plus 16?
check.why: 9 plus 16 makes 25, which is 5 times 5, the square of the long side.

check.q: What does the tablet Plimpton 322 show?
choices: The rule was known in Babylon long before Pythagoras
The rule was invented in London
check.why: Plimpton 322, from ancient Babylon, lists number sets that fit the rule more than a thousand years before Pythagoras.

lessons.title: What We Know and What We Were Told
lessons.mainIdea: Most stories about Pythagoras were written hundreds of years after he died, so historians sort them into likely facts and legends.
reading: Most of what we read about Pythagoras was written 600 to 800 years after he lived. Writers such as Iamblichus, around 300 CE, collected old stories. Some stories may be true. Others grew bigger with each telling. A story that is told for a long time but cannot be proven is a *legend*.

One legend says a member named Hippasus shared a math secret with outsiders. In the story, the group punished him. Historians treat this as a legend. It comes only from late writers, and no earlier record backs it up.

Some things are better supported. The historian Polybius wrote in the 100s BCE that Pythagorean meeting places in southern Italy were burned. So the group seems to have faced real anger from its neighbors. But even Polybius wrote hundreds of years later, and the dates are still debated. Historians call a source written long after the events a *late source*.

words.d: a story told for a long time that cannot be proven true
a source written long after the events it describes

look.title: Sort the Stories
look.text: Card A: Pythagoras was born on the island of Samos. Card B: A member named Hippasus was punished for sharing a math secret. Card C: Polybius wrote that Pythagorean meeting places were burned. Card D: A Babylonian tablet shows the triangle rule is older than Pythagoras.
look.prompt: Sort the cards into two piles: well supported, or legend. Explain one choice using the reading.

check.q: About how long after Pythagoras did writers like Iamblichus live?
check.why: The reading says most stories were written 600 to 800 years after Pythagoras lived.

check.q: Why do historians treat the Hippasus story as a legend?
choices: It comes only from late writers with no earlier record
It is carved on a mosaic
check.why: The story comes only from late writers, and no earlier record backs it up.

check.q: What did Polybius write about the Pythagoreans?
choices: Their meeting places in southern Italy were burned
They built the church of San Clemente
check.why: Polybius wrote that Pythagorean meeting places in southern Italy were burned.

review.why: Tertullian was a Christian writer who opposed the religion, so we read his story with care.

review.why: Most stories come from late sources, written 600 to 800 years later, so some are legends.
